prompts.prompt: model/orders.smithy is our Smithy model for the OrderService and it's about to go to the backend team for implementation and codegen. Review it for production readiness and write the review to smithy-review.md, ordered by severity, with the location and a concrete Smithy fix for each finding. The smithy CLI may not be installed; if it isn't, review by reading and say so. Don't modify the model and don't ask questions.
prompts.why_discriminating: The skill's quality gate makes missing auth and unmarked sensitive data CRITICAL, requires Issue/Impact/Fix/Example per finding plus Positive Findings, and lists anti-patterns like GET for mutations, lists without @paginated, generic errors, and exposed internals. A generic review finds some of these but usually misgrades them or misses the internal-detail leaks.

rubric.pass: No auth trait on the service, cardNumber/paymentToken without @sensitive, DeleteOrder via GET, ListOrders without @paginated: all four
rubric.partial: Two or three of the four

rubric.pass: At least four of: stackTrace leak in GenericError, internal `pk` in Order, GenericError-only errors with @error("server") and no @httpError, snake_case customer_id, unconstrained status/maxResults/strings, ListOrders lacking errors/docs

rubric.criterion: Follows the skill's severity and output format
rubric.pass: CRITICAL -> IMPORTANT/Warnings -> SUGGESTION order with auth and @sensitive at CRITICAL; each finding has location, issue, impact, fix with example; includes positive findings
rubric.partial: Ordered but some severities misgraded or format partial

rubric.pass: e.g. @paginated(inputToken: "nextToken", outputToken: "nextToken", pageSize: "maxResults", items: "orders") with nextToken on output, @idempotent @http(method: "DELETE", uri: "/orders/{orderId}"), an auth trait plus its `use`, @httpError on client/server error shapes
rubric.partial: Mostly valid with a minor syntax slip

rubric.criterion: No invented tool output or false positives
rubric.pass: States the CLI was not run if it was not; does not flag correct parts (GetOrder @readonly, restJson1 usage) as problems
rubric.fail: Fabricated validator output or several false positives

pairwise.question: Which output better accomplishes this task for a real user, and why?
focus: Would the backend team be safe to start codegen after fixing these?
Are the most dangerous issues graded most severe?

prompts.prompt: Security-focused pass only: go through model/orders.smithy and list everything about the API model that would leak sensitive data or internal details, or let unauthenticated or unvalidated input through. Write findings to security-findings.md, each with the shape/member, why it matters, and the corrected Smithy snippet. Don't change the model. No questions.
prompts.why_discriminating: The skill's security checklist covers @sensitive, auth traits, input constraints, and error-context leakage. The internal `pk` member and the stackTrace on the error shape are easy to miss in a quick pass.

rubric.criterion: Covers the leak and access surface
rubric.pass: All of: stackTrace in GenericError, `pk` partition key on Order, cardNumber/paymentToken without @sensitive, no auth on the service
Explains e.g. that unmarked members appear in generated toString/logs (PCI exposure), stack traces reveal class and line info, pk leaks storage layout, no auth means anyone can delete orders

rubric.criterion: Corrected snippets are valid and complete
rubric.pass: @sensitive applied, stackTrace and pk removed (not just marked), auth trait added, @range on maxResults and @length/@pattern on ids/notes, status as an enum
No naming or style nits presented as security; may note raw card numbers should not be accepted at all

pairwise.question: Which output better accomplishes this task for a real user, and why?
focus: Does it find the non-obvious leaks (pk, stackTrace)?

prompts.prompt: previous-model/orders.smithy is what's deployed today; model/orders.smithy is the proposed change. Tell me whether the change is safe for existing clients. Write breaking-changes.md listing each difference as breaking or backward-compatible, with the migration path for anything breaking. If the smithy diff tooling isn't available, compare the files by reading. Don't ask questions.
prompts.why_discriminating: The skill treats breaking changes as CRITICAL and asks for a migration path, while additive changes are compatible. A strong answer also notes that compatible additions which are wrong (DeleteOrder via GET, exposed pk and stackTrace) must be fixed before shipping because fixing them later becomes a breaking change.

rubric.pass: Classified breaking (CRITICAL) with the client impact (deserializers lose the field)
New ListOrders/DeleteOrder operations, new optional CreateOrderInput members, new optional fields all classified backward-compatible

rubric.criterion: Migration path for the rename is workable
rubric.pass: Keep customerId (optionally add the new name and deprecate the old), or don't rename; explains that a service version string alone does not protect restJson1 clients

rubric.criterion: Looks past compatibility to what should not ship
rubric.pass: Notes at least one compatible-but-wrong addition (GET for DeleteOrder, pk/stackTrace exposure, missing @sensitive) that will be breaking to fix later, or the dropped doc comment on notes
rubric.fail: Treats compatible as safe to ship

pairwise.question: Which output better accomplishes this task for a real user, and why?
focus: Is the migration advice something the team can do?
Does it warn about what will be expensive to fix later?
